panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Patient liver histology (H&E) explicitly captioned as hepatocellular adenoma with glycogen-laden hepatocytes and steatosis in a confirmed GSD-Ia case; glycogen-laden hepatocytes are a core histologic manifestation of GSD type I. [raw subtype: GSD Ia (von Gierke disease)] B: PAS stain of the patient's liver showing abundant magenta glycogen deposition, explicitly attributed by the caption to GSD-Ia-associated hepatocellular adenoma; direct confirmation of the target disease. [raw subtype: GSD Ia (von Gierke disease)]

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Shows abdominal CT evidence of hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, consistent with case presentation of GSD Type Ia. B: CT shows multiple varices in the left upper abdomen, a vascular complication mentioned in the context of this GSD Type Ia case. C: Displays a cystic mass in the spleen, consistent with pathology observed in GSD Type Ia patients. D: Shows CT findings suggestive of chronic pancreatitis and splenic vein obstruction, part of the severe presentation of this GSD case.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A shows liver histology (H&E) demonstrating extensive steatosis (fat globules). This finding is attributed to the patient with GSD Type Ia, which presents with various metabolic abnormalities including hepatic steatosis. B: Panel B displays a PAS stain of the liver biopsy, showing magenta coloration highlighted by an arrow, which is the hallmark of glycogen accumulation characteristic of GSD Ia.

Targeted and background biopsies were obtained, which showed macrovesicular steatosis without fibrosis but no definitive features of adenoma (Figure 2A). Therefore, goal of management was directed on treatment of fatty liver disease using lifestyle modifications and initiation of glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) medications given associated obesity, acanthosis nigricans, and co‐morbidities. ALT trended downward from 423 to 160 U/L following therapy, however with the MRI findings concerning for HCAs, a referral to genetics was made.

Notably, the initial biopsy staining panel did not include a Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS) stain, as normal hepatocytes inherently contain PAS‐positive glycogen. Histologic confirmation of GSD Ia typically involves PAS staining, which highlights glycogen and glycoproteins with a magenta coloration (Figure 2B), followed by diastase digestion to cleave glycogen and eliminate the magenta staining, thereby confirming glycogen accumulation. PAS stain was later included (Figure 2B), however the family declined any repeat biopsy. 10
